title: RISC vs CISC
summary: The two design philosophies behind every ISA, why RISC emerged, and how modern x86 quietly blurs the line.

slides.subTitle: CISC — do more per instruction
slides.markdown:
**CISC** (Complex Instruction Set Computer) packs rich functionality into single instructions — a single x86 instruction can load from memory, do arithmetic, and store the result back, all in one encoded operation.

The pitch: fewer instructions per program, and instructions that map closely to high-level operations, which mattered when memory was tiny and expensive and assembly was often written by hand.

The cost: instructions vary wildly in length and complexity, which makes the hardware that decodes them correspondingly complex.

slides.subTitle: RISC — simple, uniform instructions
slides.markdown:
**RISC** (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) keeps instructions simple, fixed-length, and uniform. Crucially, it's a **load/store architecture**: only dedicated load/store instructions touch memory — arithmetic instructions work strictly on registers.

An ARM or RISC-V `add` never reads memory directly; you load values into registers first, then add. This uniformity is the whole point — every instruction is easy to decode in one predictable shape.

The trade: a task that's one CISC instruction might take two or three RISC instructions instead.

RISC wasn't philosophy for its own sake — it was a bet on **pipelining**. A pipeline overlaps fetch/decode/execute across instructions, but that only works smoothly if every instruction is roughly the same shape and predictable in timing.

Variable-length, wildly-different CISC instructions make pipelining messy: the hardware often can't tell where the next instruction starts until it's finished decoding the current one.

Fixed-length, uniform RISC instructions sidestep that — the decoder always knows the next instruction boundary in advance, so the pipeline stays full.

slides.subTitle: The core trade-off
slides.markdown:
The interview-standard comparison:

| | CISC | RISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction count per program | Fewer | More |
| Cycles per instruction | Higher, variable | Lower, ~uniform |
| Instruction length | Variable | Fixed |
| Memory access | Any instruction can touch memory | Only load/store |
| Decode hardware | Complex | Simple |
| Examples | x86, x86-64 | ARM, RISC-V, MIPS |

Neither wins on raw instruction count or raw cycle count alone — total time is instructions × cycles-per-instruction × cycle time, and both families land in similar places for real workloads.

slides.subTitle: x86's RISC core
slides.markdown:
Modern x86 chips are CISC on the *outside* only. Internally, the front-end **decodes each CISC instruction into one or more simple micro-ops (μops)** that look and behave like RISC instructions — fixed shape, easy to schedule and pipeline.

This is why x86 competes on performance with RISC designs despite its complex public ISA: the complexity is absorbed at decode time, and everything downstream (scheduling, execution, retirement) is RISC-like.

The visible ISA and the internal engine have quietly diverged.

slides.subTitle: One instruction, several micro-ops
slides.markdown:
A single complex x86 instruction can expand into several internal micro-ops before it ever reaches execution:

![x86 front-end decoding one CISC instruction into several RISC-like micro-ops](assets/cisc-to-uops.svg)

The decoder is where CISC's complexity gets absorbed — everything past that stage (scheduler, execution units, reorder buffer) operates on simple, uniform micro-ops, just like a RISC pipeline would.

slides.subTitle: "RISC means faster"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "RISC chips are inherently faster than CISC chips."

**Why it's wrong:** RISC reduces cycles-per-instruction but usually needs more instructions to do the same work; CISC does the opposite. Which wins depends on the compiler's code generation, the workload, and — critically — the microarchitecture, not the label.

**Correct model:** modern x86 (CISC) and ARM (RISC) chips compete in the same performance tier for most workloads, because x86 internally executes RISC-like micro-ops. "RISC vs CISC" predicts design trade-offs, not a performance winner.
